explanations.explanation: That's the one. Some people say, “John the Baptist has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him.” (Mark 6:14) Notice it's only what people are saying. Rumors travel fast, friend, and this one is about to land in the ear of a king.

Moses, Israel's leader, isn't named here at all. The people name John the Baptist as the man risen from the dead (Mark 6:14). Others toss out Elijah or a prophet of old (Mark 6:15), but nobody in this verse says Moses. That's a lot of theories for one Jesus.

Samuel, the prophet who anointed Israel's first kings (1 Samuel 10:1), doesn't come up in this passage. The people say, “John the Baptist has risen from the dead!” (Mark 6:14) That's the name in the rumor. Good guess for a prophet, though, because the crowd was guessing prophets all over the place.

Brother is right. The text says Herod ordered John arrested “on account of his brother Philip’s wife Herodias, whom Herod had married.” (Mark 6:17) So Philip, Herod's brother, was her husband first. I'd say that family tree needed a map.
Uncle is a fun guess, but the text doesn't say it. Mark 6:17 says Philip was Herod's brother, and Herodias was Philip's wife. Herod married her. One brother, one wife, one big problem.

Cousin doesn't show up in this verse. The text says “his brother Philip’s wife Herodias, whom Herod had married.” (Mark 6:17) So Philip is Herod's brother. Close family, friend, and that's exactly why John spoke up.

explanations.answer: Herod has no right to marry Herodias
explanations.explanation: Right on the money. John had been telling Herod, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!” (Mark 6:18) He said it to a king's face. That took some courage, and I can't even tell my own mustache to settle down.

explanations.answer: Herod has no right to rule Galilee
explanations.explanation: That's not what John said. Mark 6:18 gives his words: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!” His complaint was about Herod and Herodias. The text says nothing about Herod's rule over Galilee in John's message.

explanations.answer: Herod has no right to tax the temple
explanations.explanation: Taxes never come up in this passage. John's words were, “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!” (Mark 6:18) The trouble was about Herod's marriage. This one is just not in the text, friend.

Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite. Herodias “held a grudge against John and wanted to kill him.” (Mark 6:19) She didn't let it go. That grudge is where the heavy part of this story starts to build.

That's right. John said Herod's marriage wasn't lawful (Mark 6:18), and Herodias did not shrug it off. She held a grudge and wanted to kill him (Mark 6:19). Some people let a thing go, and some people hold it tight for years.

explanations.answer: Herod feared John and protected him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Herod “feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man.” (Mark 6:20) So the same king who locked John up was also the one shielding him. I think that's a strange mix, and the text just lets it sit there.
The text doesn't say that. It says Herod feared John and protected him (Mark 6:20). Nothing in this passage puts John's disciples at the prison. They show up later, and for a very different reason.

explanations.answer: The prison guards refused her orders
explanations.explanation: Nothing about guards refusing orders is in the text. What stopped Herodias was that Herod “feared John and protected him.” (Mark 6:20) She wanted it done, but Herod stood in the way. The guards never enter the picture.

True. Mark 6:20 says that when Herod heard John's words, “he was greatly perplexed; yet he listened to him gladly.” Confused and still coming back for more. I know that feeling, like the time I read a recipe three times and kept reading.
Not this time, friend. The text says Herod “was greatly perplexed; yet he listened to him gladly.” (Mark 6:20) The word yet matters there. Confusion didn't keep him away from John's words.

explanations.answer: Whatever she asks up to half his kingdom
explanations.explanation: Yes. Herod swore to her, “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!” (Mark 6:23) He had already said she could ask for whatever she wished (Mark 6:22). That's a wide-open offer, and an oath on top of it.

explanations.answer: A palace of her own anywhere in Galilee
explanations.explanation: A palace sounds big, but it's not what the text says. Herod swore, “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!” (Mark 6:23) No palace is mentioned. His offer was a lot bigger than one building.

explanations.answer: Gold and jewels from the royal treasury
explanations.explanation: Gold and jewels aren't in this passage. Herod said, “Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!” (Mark 6:23) He didn't name a prize. He left the door wide open, and that's what makes the next part so heavy.

That's right. She went out and asked her mother, “What should I request?” (Mark 6:24) Herodias, the woman Herod had married, had held a grudge against John (Mark 6:19). I think this is the part where my own mustache goes still.

Chuza, who managed Herod's household (Luke 8:3), isn't in this scene. The text says the girl asked her mother (Mark 6:24). Chuza's name is in a different passage. He didn't get a call this time, friend.

Manaen, who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch (Acts 13:1), isn't named in this passage. Mark 6:24 says she went out and asked her mother. Different people, different passage. It was her mother she asked.
Not quite. The text says, “At once the girl hurried back to the king.” (Mark 6:25) No long pause, no pondering. She had her answer and she moved.

Right. She did not take her time. “At once the girl hurried back to the king with her request.” (Mark 6:25) She even asked for it “immediately.” Some people take forever at the snooze button, and this was the opposite.
Sorrow it is. “The king was consumed with sorrow.” (Mark 6:26) That's a heavy moment, friend. He felt it, and the text tells us so.
Relief isn't what the text says. It says, “The king was consumed with sorrow.” (Mark 6:26) That's a heavy feeling, so I'll just say it plainly. Sorrow filled Herod when he heard her request.
The text doesn't say anger. It says, “The king was consumed with sorrow.” (Mark 6:26) Sorrow is the word Mark uses. It's a hard part of the story, and I'm not going to joke about it.

explanations.answer: Because of his oaths and his guests
explanations.explanation: That's it. “Because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her.” (Mark 6:26) He had sworn in front of the leading men of Galilee (Mark 6:21-23). I think that's a sad thing to be stuck on, a promise made too fast.

explanations.answer: Because he feared what Herodias would do
explanations.explanation: Fear of Herodias isn't the reason the text gives. Mark 6:26 says, “because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her.” The text names his oaths and his guests. It doesn't say he was afraid of Herodias.

explanations.answer: Because John had insulted the girl
explanations.explanation: The text never says John insulted the girl. Herod didn't want to refuse her “because of his oaths and his guests.” (Mark 6:26) John's words were about Herod's marriage (Mark 6:18). They weren't aimed at her.

True. The man “brought John’s head on a platter and presented it to the girl, who gave it to her mother.” (Mark 6:28) This is one of the heaviest parts, friend. I think we can sit with that for a second.
The text says otherwise. The man presented it to the girl, “who gave it to her mother.” (Mark 6:28) She passed it right along to Herodias. This is a heavy part, so I'll keep it simple.

explanations.answer: Take his body and lay it in a tomb
explanations.explanation: That's right. “When John’s disciples heard about this, they came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.” (Mark 6:29) After all that darkness, there are people who came to care for him. That's a quiet, faithful thing, and I'm glad Mark tells us.

explanations.answer: Go to Herod's palace to confront him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. It says John's disciples “came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.” (Mark 6:29) There's no trip to the palace in these verses. They cared for John's body.

explanations.answer: Scatter and hide far outside Galilee
explanations.explanation: Scattering isn't what the text says. John's disciples “came and took his body and placed it in a tomb.” (Mark 6:29) They came to him, not away from him. That's the part Mark gives us.
